summary: Get-ImportRuleNames now returns each import-rule name spelt the way the harness's say() prints it. The python -c code applies `.encode('ascii', 'backslashreplace').decode('ascii')` to each name before json.dumps, so a character past ASCII reaches C-007 as its escape (\xe9, —), exactly as it appears in the harness output. Shape-ImportRuleNames gains a probe named with an e-acute and an em dash; the characters are built with [char] so the test file stays ASCII. The shape passes under both hosts with 9 import rules named. With the encode removed it exits 1 and reports exactly that probe as unnamed. This is the fourth finding in a row on the same name comparison (R2-m2, m3, R2-m4, m5); each one was a real mismatch between two spellings written in this slice, and follow_ups names the structural close.

files.why: O-028: Get-ImportRuleNames' python -c now emits r['name'].encode('ascii','backslashreplace').decode('ascii'), the spelling harness.py's say() prints, and its comment says so. The file stays ASCII: a stray em dash that went into the comment was replaced before finishing, and 0 non-ASCII bytes remain.

O-028: Shape-ImportRuleNames adds the probe "the provider's caf{E-ACUTE} probe {EM-DASH} never imports Core". The placeholders become [char]0xE9 and [char]0x2014 at run time, so the file stays ASCII under powershell.exe 5.1's ANSI read. The comment lists the new spelling.

follow_ups: Loop: R2-m2, m3, R2-m4 and m5 are four findings in a row against one comparison: C-007 re-derives each import-rule name and looks for it as quoted text in the harness's human-readable summary line. Each fix was correct, but each makes the two independently written spellings agree on one more axis (quoting, wrapping, yaml syntax, now console escaping), so the next axis can always be named. A structural close is for the harness to also print one machine-readable line, e.g. `harness: not-run-json [...]` with json.dumps(names) (ASCII by default), and for C-007 to compare that list, parsed, against the engine-parsed yaml list. That removes the text-spelling layer from the comparison altogether. It touches harness.py's output contract, so a person should rank it rather than a reviewer filing a fifth instance.
